title: Nakhon Sawan Chinese New Year: Dragon Parade Itinerary
metaDesc: A day-by-day plan for Thailand's biggest Chinese New Year festival in Pak Nam Pho, Nakhon Sawan. Catch the night and day god parades, pray at the shrines, eat old-school Chinese food, plus parade-viewing spots and hotel-booking tips.
keywords: Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year, Nakhon Sawan Chinese New Year, Pak Nam Pho god parade, Nakhon Sawan festival, golden dragon Pak Nam Pho
h1:
Chinese New Year in Pak Nam Pho
Dragon Parades, Shrines & Chinese Food
intro: It only happens once a year. The Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year is the biggest and oldest god parade festival in Thailand, running for more than a century. The whole town turns red, with golden dragons, lion dances, Eng Kor warriors, and the Hainanese bowl dance filling the streets. This plan is built as a block-by-block day: arrive a day before the parades to walk the shrines and try the Chinese food, then catch both the night and day parade highlights in full. We'll also be straight with you about the two hardest parts of visiting now — finding a room and finding parking.

blocks.html: If you want Nakhon Sawan at its liveliest, come during the Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year. This isn't just praying at a shrine — it's a full god parade festival that pulls in the whole town plus visitors from all over the country. This year (2026) is the 110th edition, running from 10–21 February 2026, a full 12 days and 12 nights, under the theme "110 Years of Colourful Chinese New Year, City of Five Languages." The two days everyone waits for are the big parades: the night parade (Chiu Sa) on 19 Feb and the day parade (Chiu Si) on 20 Feb. So this plan has you arriving the evening before the parades and staying two nights to catch both.

One note before we start: the Chinese New Year dates shift with the lunar calendar every year, usually landing somewhere between late January and February. If you're reading this in a different year, check the latest schedule from the "Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year" page or TAT Nakhon Sawan before planning. The main events and the order of ceremonies stay much the same year to year.

blocks.text: What is this festival, and why is it the biggest in Thailand?

blocks.html: Going back over a hundred years, the Pak Nam Pho market was hit hard by a cholera outbreak — a lot of people died. The Chinese community in the market brought the city gods out and paraded them around town to drive away the disease. When the outbreak settled, that act of faith turned into a tradition that has carried on every year since. Several Chinese groups — Cantonese, Hakka, Teochew, and Hainanese — each brought their own art forms, which is why the Pak Nam Pho parade has lion dances, dragons, Eng Kor, drum-and-cymbal troupes, and the bowl dance all in one festival.

The main deities the people of Pak Nam Pho honour are Chao Pho Thepharak, Chao Pho Guan Yu (Guan Gong), Chao Mae Thapthim, and Chao Mae Sawan. They sit in two shrines: the Chao Pho Thepharak shrine on the Chao Phraya River by the Pak Nam Pho market, and the Chao Mae Na Pha shrine on the Ping River just north of the market. These two shrines are the heart of the festival. On parade days the deities are carried out of the shrines on palanquins and paraded along the streets so people can pay their respects and pray from the roadside.

items: The golden dragon — the highlight everyone waits for. A dragon dozens of metres long winding down the street, handlers running in sync with the drums, with fire-breathing in some stretches. Fun for kids and adults alike.
The lion dance — several lion troupes leaping for ang pao (red envelopes) and climbing flower-pole stacks. Every move keeps you on edge.
The Eng Kor — performers paint their faces to channel Chinese heroes, carrying staffs and marching in formation with a fierce stance. It's a signature of this festival.

Drum troupes and the Hainanese bowl dance — drum and cymbal bands set the rhythm for the whole parade, while the Hainanese bowl dance (rum thuai) is an old performance you'll rarely see anywhere else.
The deity palanquins — the gods are carried on palanquins down the street, with people lining both sides at altar tables waiting to greet the procession.

blocks.text: Day 0 — Arrive the evening before, walk the shrines, taste the Chinese food

blocks.html: Arriving a day before the parades makes everything easier. You check in before the crowds pile in, explore the town, scope out a viewing spot, and pray at the shrines without being shoulder to shoulder with the crowd. By this point the Pak Nam Pho market is already decked out in red lanterns — it photographs beautifully.

blocks.label: Day 0
blocks.title: Evening before the parade — pray, walk the market, taste Chinese food

items.activity: Arrive in Pak Nam Pho, check into a hotel in town, drop your bags, and head out on foot
items.note: Pick a place in the town centre or near the Pak Nam Pho market so you can walk to the parade route. Traffic is heavy during the festival and parking is hard to find.

items.activity: Head to the Chao Pho Thepharak shrine on the Chao Phraya River — the centre of the festival — to light incense and pray
items.note: The shrine is decorated for the festival, with stations for changing into a red shirt and for warding off bad luck. Dress modestly.

items.activity: Walk along the Pak Nam Pho market to see the red lanterns, the Chinese gateway arches, and the shops selling offerings and ang pao
items.note: This is the area to watch the parade the next day. Walking it now helps you figure out where to stand.

items.activity: Dinner at one of the town's old Chinese restaurants, or original dumplings, steamed buns, and dim sum
items.note: Pak Nam Pho has Chinese restaurants passed down over generations. It gets busy during Chinese New Year, so go before 7pm or call to book a table.

items.activity: Sit at a café or drinks spot along the Pak Nam Pho embankment, catch the river breeze, and soak up the mood before the festival proper
items.note: The riverside is cool in the evening — an easy walk to settle your dinner.

blocks.title: Tip for praying at the shrines
blocks.html: If you're serious about coming to pray, you can bring your own incense, candles, fruit, and red envelopes — or just buy a ready-made offering set at the shops in front of the shrine. Avoid the late morning of parade days because it's packed; come to pray the evening before for a calmer atmosphere.

blocks.text: Day 1 — The night parade (Chiu Sa), the highlight night

blocks.html: The night parade, or "Chiu Sa" (19 Feb in 2026), is the one a lot of people love most, because the lit-up dragons and lions run through the dark with fireworks and coloured lights — a real spectacle. Rest during the day to save your energy, eat your way through the festival stalls, then go claim a viewing spot from early evening.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Rest in the morning, walk the festival in the afternoon, watch the night parade

items.activity: An easy morning — dim sum, congee, and pa thong ko (Chinese doughnuts), then a stroll along the river
items.note: Save your energy for tonight, when you'll be standing to watch the parade for a long time.

items.activity: Stop by the Chao Mae Na Pha shrine on the Ping River north of the market, the festival's other main shrine
items.note: A different feel from the Chao Pho Thepharak shrine — the Ping riverside is quieter and good for photos.

items.activity: Lunch on the town's signature dishes: knife-fish ball noodles, or Ko Yom steamed rice-skin dumpling noodles
items.note: Knife fish and the steamed rice-skin dumplings are Pak Nam Pho's hometown dishes. Popular shops sell out fast, so going before 1pm is the safer bet.

items.activity: Walk the festival stalls and try the Chinese street food — pastries, sticky rice cakes (khanom khaeng), mochi, and Chinese New Year toys
items.note: During the festival there's a market and food stalls running the whole length of the route. Taste a little of everything.

items.activity: Claim a spot for the night parade from early evening, picking a place along the route the procession passes
items.note: Arrive at least an hour before the parade starts to grab a good spot. Around the Chao Pho Thepharak shrine and the main streets are the most crowded.

items.activity: Watch the night parade — the lit-up golden dragon, lions, Eng Kor, fireworks, and the deity palanquins
items.note: The parade runs for several hours, so there's no rush. Watch the fun stretches, then move on. Watch your valuables in the crush.

items.activity: Head back to your hotel gradually, stopping for a late-night snack near the market
items.note: After the parade everyone leaves at once and traffic backs up. Walking back to a nearby hotel beats driving.

blocks.title: Making the most of the night parade
blocks.html: If you're bringing young kids or older relatives, pick a spot with a seat or a kerb where you can stand for a long stretch. Bring water and a hand fan, because standing for a long time in a crowd can get hot. To get a good shot of the lit-up dragon, turn on your phone's night mode and find a spot where the street lights don't glare back into the camera.

blocks.text: Day 2 — The day parade (Chiu Si), then grab some souvenirs

blocks.html: The day parade, or "Chiu Si" (20 Feb in 2026), is a big procession where you see the details more clearly than at night — the bright costumes, the outfits, the Hainanese bowl dance, and the deity palanquins passing by for people on both sides to pay their respects. If you like photos where you can actually see faces, the day parade is easier to shoot.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Watch the day parade, make a farewell prayer, buy souvenirs to take home

items.activity: Wake up early, have a light breakfast, then claim a spot along the day-parade route
items.note: People come early for the day parade too. Arriving early gets you a shaded spot with a clear view.

items.activity: Watch the day parade — the Hainanese bowl dance, lions, dragon, Eng Kor, and the deity palanquins
items.note: Bring a hat or sun umbrella. The sun is strong during the day parade, so drink water often.

items.activity: Stop at the Chao Pho Thepharak shrine for a farewell prayer before you go, to close out the trip
items.note: Many people make a point of praying both at the start and at the end, for good luck.

items.activity: A farewell lunch — a well-known red pork rice or roast duck rice shop, or a riverside fish restaurant
items.note: Choose a place off the parade route so you don't have to wait long. Shops near the festival are packed right now.

items.activity: Buy souvenirs — Pak Nam Pho mochi, daifuku, knife-fish balls, and Chinese New Year sweets
items.note: The old mochi shops are around Sawan Withi Road. They sell well during Chinese New Year, so go a bit earlier to get the full range.
Avoid leaving at the same time as the whole festival. Heading out in the early afternoon, or waiting until the evening once the crowds thin, means lighter traffic.

blocks.title: On parking and getting around during the festival
blocks.html: During Chinese New Year, many streets in town are closed for the parades — cars can't get through and parking fills up fast. If you're driving in yourself, park outside the festival zone and walk in, or stay at a hotel with its own parking. Check the road-closure announcements from the festival page ahead of time so you can plan your parking better.

blocks.text: Festival Chinese food you have to try

blocks.html: The Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year is heaven for anyone who loves to eat, between the festival stalls and the old-school shops in the market. Here are the Chinese dishes people recommend most when you come during the festival.

items.name: Knife-fish ball noodles
items.blurb: The town's signature. Bouncy fish balls made from real knife fish, in a clear broth — even better with a side of knife-fish cake. This is the first dish Pak Nam Pho locals will point you to.
items.meta: Old fish shops in the market · open morning to afternoon

items.name: Ko Yom steamed rice-skin dumpling noodles
items.blurb: Soft rice skin wrapped around a generous filling, steamed fresh, dressed with dipping sauce and crispy pork. A local specialty that's hard to find elsewhere — try the tom yum version too.

items.name: Dim sum — dumplings & steamed buns
items.blurb: Old dim sum shops in the Pak Nam Pho market, served piping hot with tea in the morning. During Chinese New Year the queues are long.

items.name: Red pork rice & roast duck rice
items.blurb: Shops passed down over generations. Sweet, fragrant red pork with a rich sauce, and tender five-spice braised duck — homestyle Chinese food the locals actually eat.

items.name: Pak Nam Pho mochi & daifuku
items.blurb: The town's signature souvenir — soft mochi dough with mung bean, sesame, or custard filling. The original shops are around Sawan Withi Road, perfect to take home as a Chinese New Year gift.

items.name: Sticky rice cakes, khanom thian & Chinese pastries
items.blurb: Auspicious Chinese New Year sweets, sold all over the market during the festival — both to eat and to offer to the gods. The mung bean and salted egg pastries are fragrant and rich.

blocks.text: Where to stay during Chinese New Year

blocks.html: Chinese New Year in Pak Nam Pho is the town's high season — hotels in the centre fill up fast and prices climb above normal. If you're coming, book several weeks ahead. The best location is in the town centre near the parade route, because you can walk to the festival and don't have to gamble on traffic.

items.name: In town near the Pak Nam Pho market
items.blurb: Walk to the shrines and the parade route, and get back to your hotel easily after the night parade. The best fit for this plan, but rooms are hard to get — book quickly.

items.name: Hotels with their own parking
items.blurb: Parking is very scarce during the festival. A hotel with its own lot cuts out a big headache if you're driving in.

blocks.text: Which part of the festival suits whom

items: Night parade (Chiu Sa) — for people who love the atmosphere, fireworks, lights, and energy. The lit-up dragon is the most dazzling, but it's crowded and hot.
Day parade (Chiu Si) — for people who like detailed photos: costumes and the bowl dance are clearer, and it suits older relatives and kids, but you'll need sun protection.

Weekdays during the festival (10–18 Feb) — for people who don't want the crowds. You can pray, walk the market, watch the stage performances, and taste the food more comfortably, and rooms are easier to find than on the two parade days.
Coming with a big family — stay in town, focus on walking around, avoid driving into the festival zone, and set a meeting point in case anyone gets separated in the crowd.

blocks.html: Here's a rough two-night budget per person during Chinese New Year, not counting travel to Nakhon Sawan. Accommodation costs more during the festival, around 900–1,800 THB per room per night (cheaper once split). Food and festival snacks for the whole trip run around 600–1,000 THB. Offerings and souvenirs are up to you, around 300–600 THB. All in, two nights comes to roughly 1,800–3,000 THB per person, depending on how early you managed to book your room.

faq.q: When is the Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year in 2026?
faq.a: It runs from 10–21 February 2026, a full 12 days and 12 nights, and this is the 110th edition. The highlights are the night parade (Chiu Sa) on 19 Feb and the day parade (Chiu Si) on 20 Feb. The Chinese New Year dates shift with the lunar calendar every year, so for other years check the latest schedule from the festival page or TAT first.

faq.q: What's the difference between the night and day parades?
faq.a: The night parade (Chiu Sa) has lit-up dragons and lions, fireworks, and coloured lights — a lively spectacle. The day parade (Chiu Si) shows the costume detail, the Hainanese bowl dance, and the deity palanquins more clearly, and it's easier to photograph. If you have the time, watch both days.

faq.q: Where's the best spot to watch the parade?
faq.a: The main route runs through the Pak Nam Pho market area and the main streets around the Chao Pho Thepharak shrine — the most crowded but with the clearest view. Come to claim a spot at least an hour before the parade starts, and pick a kerb where you can stand for a while. Check that year's parade route on the festival page first, as it's adjusted slightly some years.

faq.q: What festival Chinese food should I try?
faq.a: Start with the knife-fish ball noodles and the Ko Yom steamed rice-skin dumpling noodles, the town's hometown dishes, then follow up with dim sum, red pork rice and roast duck rice, and auspicious Chinese New Year sweets like sticky rice cakes and Chinese pastries. For souvenirs, take home Pak Nam Pho mochi and daifuku.

faq.q: Are rooms hard to find during Chinese New Year?
faq.a: They're hard to find and pricier than usual, because it's the town's high season, especially on the two big parade days. Book several weeks ahead. Choosing a place in town near the parade route is the most convenient, and if you're driving in yourself, find a hotel with its own parking lot, because parking in the festival zone fills up very fast.
